title: Setting up a scroll frame
subtitle: How to lace and tension fabric in a two-roller scroll frame.
excerpt: A scroll frame mounts fabric between two dowel rods and keeps it under even tension. The fabric is laced to the side bars to stop it rolling in. Scroll frames suit long pieces, large embroideries, and any work requiring precise stitch tension.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Frame embroidery chapter, scroll and roller frames.

glossaryTerms.definition: An embroidery frame with two parallel dowel rods joined by side bars. Fabric is stitched or taped to the rods, which roll to expose different sections of a long piece. The side bars lace tightly to keep the fabric square.

content.text: holds fabric under consistent, even tension without the risk of hoop-mark distortion. It is the standard frame for large embroideries, canvas work, and any piece where maintaining straight grain through the whole project is important.

items.name: Strong thread or twine for lacing the side bars
Herringbone or twill tape, stitched to the fabric edges

content.text: How to set up a scroll frame
Stitch herringbone or twill tape to the top and bottom edges of the fabric. The tape gives a sturdy edge to attach to the roller rods.
Mark the centre of each rod and the centre of each taped fabric edge.
Oversew or lace the top taped edge to the top rod, working outward from the centre on each side. Do the same with the bottom rod.
Assemble the frame by slotting the side bars into the rods. Tighten the wing nuts or pegs until the fabric is flat but not strained.
Thread a length of strong thread onto a blunt needle. Lace it through the selvedge or tape along each side of the fabric, then wrap around the side bar every 1 to 2 cm.
Pull the lacing snug on each side so the fabric stretches evenly across its width. Tie off.
Check that the grain runs straight both horizontally and vertically before you begin stitching.

items.symptom: The fabric sags in the centre
items.cause: The rods were not rolled out far enough or the side-bar lacing is too loose.
items.fix: Roll each rod outward by half a turn to increase vertical tension. Re-lace the side bars more firmly.

items.symptom: The grain is skewed at an angle
items.cause: The fabric was attached off-centre or one rod is rolled further than the other.
items.fix: Unroll both rods to the same position and re-attach from the centre outward. Check the grain against a drawn thread line.

content.text: A correctly set scroll frame is the foundation for all canvas work, goldwork, and large surface embroidery.
